newsitem.title: UK: UN decision on sanctions a blow to Libyan efforts.
newsitem.headline: UN decision on sanctions a blow to Libyan efforts.

text.p: A U.N. Security Council decision on Friday to leave sanctions against Libya in place was a major blow to the Middle East state's worldwide efforts to end the arms and air travel embargo, diplomatic sources said.
"Libya has been lobbying hard to ensure support from the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organisation of African Unity and the Arab League," an Arab diplomat told Reuters by telephone.
"Tripoli has drawn up a draft resolution which will be voted on in the General Assembly on 19 November which calls for an end to "coercive measures,'" he added.
In New York, the Security Council decided after a routine review on Friday to leave the sanctions unchanged.
Diplomatic and shipping sources in the Middle East said reports of a sanctions-busting arms trade with Iran, possibly involving parts for missiles, was behind the decision.
In September, the shipping sources in Beirut said an Iranian ship carried arms and explosives to Libya in contravention of the U.N. sanctions.

The U.N. ban was imposed after a Pan American World Airways Boeing 747 crashed on the town of Lockerbie, Scotland, killing the 259 people aboard, in December 1988. Eleven people in Lockerbie were also killed.

Investigators said Flight 103 was blown up by a bomb. They blamed two Libyan security officials, and demanded they face trial in the West. An air travel and arms embargo was imposed for Libya's failure to hand over the two suspects.

The sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the sanctions-busting ship, the Iran Ershad, made the long journey to Libya around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope rather than the normal, shorter route through the Suez Canal.
"The ship's route and size of the cargo...indicate that the shipment was probably ballistic-missile related," said one Arab diplomat who asked not to be named.

On October 7 the Libyan sanctions committee of 15 members met to discuss the issue. The chairman, Polish Permanent Representative Zbigniew Maria Wlosowicz, called on his Iranian and Libyan counterparts to respond to the reports.
There was no response, the sources said.

Libya already has Russian-made Scud B missiles with a range of about 300 km (185 miles), but military analysts in the region say it is keen to improve the weapons' range. Iran has the ability to build Scud Cs with a range of more than 500 km (300 miles) and can carry chemical or biological warheads.

Both Libya and Iraq complained bitterly to a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome on Thursday that sanctions imposed against them were unjust, criminal and contrary to the meeting's goal of stamping out hunger.
